title: Previous winter ice raised linear forecast error by 3.50% across four Great Lakes in 1994-2026
abstract: We tested whether last winter's maximum ice cover improves next-winter linear forecasts in Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. We used a fixed NOAA GLERL table for 1973-2026. Each lake model used only earlier target years. Across 33 test winters in 1994-2026, adding last winter to a year-trend model increased equal-lake mean squared error by 3.50%. The conditional 95% five-year block interval for the increase was 0.80% to 6.71%. Root mean squared error rose from 29.08 to 29.58 ice percentage points. All four lake point scores were worse. Checks without a year trend and with 20-year training windows gave intervals that included zero. This result applies to one input, model class and final data snapshot. It does not show that thermal memory is absent. Short dependent records, chart changes and conditional intervals limit inference. Code, exact source provenance, aggregate scores, simulation draws, an independent arithmetic audit and a figure are included. External annual records remain outside the package.

display.caption: Left: score summaries for 33 winters. Four-lake mean is the square root of mean squared errors, not the mean of four RMSE values. Right: MSE reduction with 95% conditional block intervals. Negative values mean worse forecasts.

citations.reason: Prior campaign ice-timing test identified and documented the shared source snapshot. Our new code tests forecast memory, not timing spread. Data overlap; this is not independent data confirmation.
Winter conditions and later heat content motivate a test of annual forecast memory. This paper does not establish next-winter ice prediction skill.
